Broken Tooling Prompts Ford F-Series Recall, 2026 and 2027 Models Affected
8 photos
Photo: Ford
Assembly line workers at Ford's Kentucky truck plant were running open-gate load tests on June 13, 2026. As part of said testing, plant operators noticed something worrying in the form of left-hand tailgate cables separating from the side eyelet. In the first instance, the Ford Motor Company hypothesized that the eyelet crimp was malformed.
The supplier, namely Ohio-based Cable Manufacturing & Assembly Co., ultimately confirmed that certain tailgate cables were produced using a broken crimping die. Potentially compromised parts were produced at the supplier's facility during two shifts on May 26, 2026, and the supplier also confirmed that only left-side cables may be compromised.
Based on audit records, approximately 600 units of these suspect cables were shipped to the second-largest automaker among the Detroit Big Three. As expected, the Ford Motor Company issued a stop-ship order for the affected 2026 and 2027 model year F-Series trucks. The recall population includes the F-150 and Super Duties, all the way to the F-450.
Ford wants to inspect no fewer than 30,123 trucks in the US market, with production dates ranging from May 30, 2026, through June 15, 2026. The F-150 is listed with the largest population of the bunch, totaling 18,412 units across the 2026 and 2027 model years. The remainder splits among heavy-duty variants, of which the F-250 accounts for 7,387 units.
FoMoCo estimates that only 2 percent of the entire population actually carries defective left-side cables. Imagine rolling a pair of motorcycles onto an open tailgate. The static weight hits both support cables. If the left-side tailgate eyelet pulls free, everything transfers to the right cable. The tailgate ultimately drops onto the rear bumper, no longer supporting the load, increasing the risk of injury.
Photo: Ford The Critical Concern Review Group analyzed this matter on June 18, 2026, and the Field Review Committee gave its blessing to recall potentially affected pickups three months later. To date, FoMoCo hasn't received a single warranty claim or field report potentially related to the recall condition.
Dealers are to swap out the suspect left-hand side tailgate cables at no charge to affected customers. The remedy units are said to be manufactured using properly calibrated tooling. Dealers will be notified about this recall, which the NHTSA refers to as 26V689, on January 11, 2027. Interim customer notifications are due this December, while remedy notifications are planned for January.
Affected vehicle identification numbers will become searchable on the federal watchdog's portal no later than December 7, 2026. FL34-9944411-AD is the part number of the subject left-hand tailgate support cable. Based on a quick Google search, this part also fits the 2021 through 2025 model year F-150.
For model year 2027, the F-150 lost its 2.7-liter EcoBoost twin-turbo V6 in favor of a 3.0-liter unit. Elsewhere, the 5.0-liter Coyote naturally aspirated V8 returns to high-end trim levels. Automatic start-stop has been removed from a bunch of models, while a new gasoline particulate filter has been introduced to the 3.5-liter EcoBoost twin-turbo V6 and its PowerBoost-branded hybrid sibling.
As far as the Super Duty is concerned, the 2027 model year saw Ford eliminate the 6.8-liter gas V8 in favor of the larger Godzilla lump. As ever, the Power Stroke turbo diesel remains the Super Duty engine to get for towing. When properly equipped, the Super Duty offers up to 40,000 pounds (18,144 kilograms) as long as customers opt for the XL Regular Cab 4x2 DRW.

Nissan Pathfinder Rendered Unrecognizable: Nismo Nick Built Twin Track and Trail Monsters
16 photos
Photo: Nismonickofficial | Instagram
Someone rendered the Nissan Pathfinder unrecognizable and is now taking it to the 2027 SEMA Show. Car builder Nicholas Scherr actually built not one, but two heavily modified Nissan Pathfinders, so meet the Trackfinder and Trailfinder, the non-identical twins that mark the 40th anniversary of the nameplate.
Nicholas Scherr, widely known as "Nismo Nick," has come up with twin builds of the R51 Nissan Pathfinder, pushing the traditional third-generation body-on-frame platform into two completely opposite directions. One is built for the road and track, while the other is designed for extreme rugged overlanding.
Both builds are finished in Ruby Slate Pearl, a signature color from Nissan's 40th Anniversary Maxima, and sport modern front- and rear-end mods, borrowed directly from the contemporary Nissan Frontier midsize pickup truck.
The Nissan Pathfinder Trackfinder will win races from stoplight to stoplight The Trackfinder is a low-slung, high-octane street build, looking like it is ready to flip the script on what a three-row family SUV actually is. It retains the factory 4.0-liter V6, codenamed VQ40DE, pushing out 266 horsepower (270 metric horsepower) and 288 pound-feet (391 Newton meters) of torque in stock form.
Photo: Nismonickofficial | Instagram However, Nismo Nick counted on the presence of a Z1 Off-Road supercharger kit and dialed it up to produce 501 rear-wheel horsepower, which translates to roughly 560 horsepower (567 metric horsepower) at the crank, which is more than double the factory rating. And that’s not all.
The factory automatic transmission is out, making room for a six-speed manual transmission, sourced from an Xterra, the rugged, truck-based compact SUV that Nissan built from 1999 through 2015, sporting a custom third-pedal master cylinder assembly. The SUV is equipped with a custom LOJ Conversions coilover system to significantly lower the ride height.
And it is not just about what is under the hood. The Trackfinder also got looks to match the extra oomph. It received a carbon fiber hood and rides on 20-inch wheels wrapped in Goodyear Eagle tires. Z1 big brakes provide the stopping power, while the aggressive centrally positioned quad-tip exhaust roars out some V6 drama.
In the meantime, the original dashboard was swapped for that of a 2022 or newer Nissan Frontier. Premium custom Katzkin leather with burgundy details, as a throwback to the 1980s original Pathfinder, covers the seats.
The Nissan Pathfinder Trailfinder will find its way out of predicament In the meantime, its non-identical twin, the Trailfinder, is a rugged off-road concept. " This is unlike any R51 Pathfinder you’ve ever seen ," says the man who created it. The go-anywhere machine is based on full-size truck mechanical underpinnings. Rather than boosting the original V6, like in the Trackfinder, Nismo Nick completed a full VK56 5.6-liter V8 engine swap, the powerplant that Nissan originally used in the Titan and the Armada.
Photo: Nismonickofficial | Instagram The V8 engine with naturally aspirated firepower now churns out roughly 400 horsepower. That same engine produced 400 horsepower (406 metric horsepower) and 413 pound-feet (560 Newton meters) of torque in the Titan and Armada .
The vehicle sits on a heavy-duty Titan-swap X-Pro suspension setup, supplied by Z1 Off-Road, and rides on massive 35-inch Hankook Dynapro AT2 Xtreme tires. The radical Pathfinder Trailfinder also features Hammerhead Armor components, an integrated front winch for the moments when the going gets tough, a snorkel, and flared bodywork.
Furthermore, the custom trunk liner cargo mat sports integrated, removable traction recovery boards that clip directly into the flooring, allowing the driver to unclip, flip, and use them in mud or snow, or whatever comes his way.
The two Pathfinders will be on display at the 2027 SEMA Show in Las Vegas. But don't go asking how much they cost, because there are no plans for the two to go into production. They are one-off, independent shop custom builds, designed and engineered to show the aftermarket tuning capabilities.
Photo: Nismonickofficial | Instagram Furthermore, they are built on the third-generation R51 Pathfinder chassis, which Nissan stopped producing back in 2012, so the automaker would by no means put the assembly lines back together just to roll out vehicles that have been out of production for nearly 15 years.
The automaker also pulled the plug on the 5.6-liter VK56 V8 engine back in 2024 to make room for the production of the VR35DDTT unit, a 3.5-liter twin-turbocharged, direct-injected V6, which now powers the Nissan Armada and Patrol, as well as the Infiniti QX80.
In the meantime, the latest Nissan Pathfinder has to deal with the 3.5-liter naturally aspirated V6, code-named VQ35DD, good for 284 horsepower and 259 pound-feet in the SV and SL trims, which start at $39,990 and $42,590, respectively, but making 295 horsepower and 270 pound-feet of torque in the range-topping Rock Creek, which is a $45,090 deal.
Every Pathfinder sold in the United States rolls off the production line of Nissan's assembly plant in Smyrna, Tennessee. Nissan sold 87,382 Pathfinders in the U.S. from January to September 2026 and is chasing the 2025 record, when it moved 101,598 units. The 2027 Alliance Pradigm 373FB Is a Couples' RV With a Massive Front Bath and Private King Bedroom
19 photos
Photo: Blue Compass RV/ That RV girl
Alliance RV may not be among the veterans of the American RV industry, but the company has made a strong name for itself in a relatively short time. Much of that success is owed to the company’s commitment to quality, innovation, and customer-driven new product development.
What the Elkhart, Indiana-based company does differently from other brands is that it listens to its clients and puts their feedback at the center of its design process. The Paradigm is one of Alliance’s most popular ranges and a perfect example of this customer-centric approach. The fifth-wheel lineup has been developed using direct input from RV owners, bringing together the features customers want most with the build quality and attention to detail Alliance is known for.
Designed specifically for long-term travel and full-time living, the Paradigm models are premium fifth-wheel RVs that deliver residential-like living comfort, year-round utility, stylish finishes, heavy-duty towing specs, and robust off-grid capabilities.
The latest addition to the range is the 2027 Paradigm 373FB, a new floor plan for the 2027 model year that stands out with a massive front bathroom with integrated laundry facilities and a mid-ship king bedroom designed as a private retreat. The fifth-wheel measures 40.9 feet (12.4 meters) in total length and sits on a 101-inch (256-cm) widebody drop-frame chassis, but despite its imposing proportions, this is essentially a couple’s RV that makes life on the road feel like home.
Photo: Blue Compass RV/ That RV girl Built on heavy-duty Curt axles, the 373FB comes with upgraded running gear featuring Touring Coil Suspension (TCS) with shock dampening, H-rated tires, and a Helux Series coil spring pin box, which will considerably smooth out your rides.
In terms of construction, the Paradigm 373FB features an aluminum frame and high-gloss fiberglass exterior with insulated laminated rear walls and a painted fiberglass front cap. Up top, a PVC roof membrane covers a fully walkable roof, while a rear ladder provides easy access to the roof.
The RV ’s exterior is equipped with practical features for prolonged stays, including two power patio awnings with integrated lighting, an LP quick-connect, a spray port by the entry door, two 30-lb propane bottles, and a 2-inch rear accessory hitch. At the front, apart from a large pass-through garage space that provides ample storage and integrates the RV’s utility center, there are also three other compartments under the front cap, providing access to various vital systems.
Photo: Blue Compass RV/ That RV girl No less than three slide-outs help create a particularly wide interior that will certainly appeal to travelers who love space. The floor plan separates the main living areas, creating privacy where it counts while keeping the lounge and kitchen connected. It puts a full-width bathroom at the front, which serves as an en-suite for the bedroom, while the kitchen and living room are toward the rear, with a bonus powder room near these open-plan common areas.
As mentioned, this is a travel trailer for couples, with a single proper bedroom, but it also gives owners the possibility to accommodate occasional guests on a fold-out sofa.
The bedroom comes standard with a king-size bed, but buyers can opt for a queen instead. Several residential touches make the room truly comfortable, such as a stylish headboard, a window above the bed, nightstands on either side, and reading lights. Under-bed storage, a flip-top dresser flanked by twin wardrobes, and a dedicated linen closet provide tons of storage. A smart TV is also included for entertainment.
Photo: Blue Compass RV/ That RV girl From the bedroom, a sliding door leads to the front bathroom, which Alliance has designed as a bath-and-spa suite. Since it spans the full width of the fifth wheel, it offers more room than the typical RV bathroom, and its fixtures are impressive. It features a large, one-piece fiberglass shower measuring 61 by 30 inches (155 by 76 cm), with a skylight above and a luxurious shower hardware set, a porcelain toilet with a soft-close seat, and a big vanity with solid-surface countertop, two undermount sinks, and generous storage.
What makes it even more impressive is a walk-in closet integrated at the very front and a dedicated closet with washer and dryer preparation, further highlighting this model’s practicality for long journeys and full-time living.
The rear area of the RV is designed as a social space. The kitchen is arranged around a beautiful kitchen island with waterfall-edged countertops and a large undermount sink. The appliance set has been chosen to deliver residential functionality and includes a Lusso range with four burners and a large oven, a microwave, and a large two-door refrigerator. For other smaller appliances, groceries, and supplies, there are two pantries - one near the half-bath and one concealed behind the entertainment wall.
Photo: Blue Compass RV/ That RV girl The lounge area is designed for more than two people to gather and spend time together. It is fitted with a pair of theater seats facing an entertainment wall with a large HD Smart TV, a soundbar, and an electric fireplace, as well as a tri-fold sleeper sofa that pulls into a guest bed. Also included is a dinette for two that expands into one for four people, and atrium windows surround the entire back area of the RV, bringing in plenty of natural light.
The Paradigm 373FB has a dry weight of 15,222 pounds (6,904 kg) and a gross vehicle weight rating of 18,000 pounds (8,164 kg), giving it a generous cargo carrying capacity of 2,778 pounds (1,260 kg). This means you can bring along tons of personal belongings, supplies, and optional equipment. As for the water tanks, the RV carries 98 gallons (370 liters) of fresh water, along with 106-gallon (400-liter) gray and black water tanks.
Photo: Blue Compass RV/ That RV girl Other nifty features that support long-term living in the RV include three air conditioners, a 40K BTU furnace, a 12-gallon gas or electric water heater, cable and satellite inputs, a 50-amp service with detachable power cord, and more. For those who want to venture off-grid, the company offers the optional SolarMax + package, which includes up to four 400W solar panels, a 1200Ah Lithium battery bank, dual Victron Charge Controllers, dual 5000W Victron Quattro inverters, and a 7-inch control panel.
MSRP for this new Alliance Paradigm fifth wheel RV has yet to be revealed.

source_document.body:
How much more generation will the U.S. need to meet rising electricity demand? It’s an important question, but it isn’t the only one the power industry needs to answer. As data centers, advanced manufacturing, and broader electrification increase demand, the growing challenge is delivering power where and when it is needed.
COMMENTARY
New generation can add capacity to the system, but it doesn’t necessarily resolve transmission constraints, interconnection delays, or periods when local demand outpaces available supply. That puts a premium on flexibility.
Energy storage can provide flexibility at multiple points across the power system, from utility-scale installations to resources deployed behind the meter at data centers and other mission-critical facilities. Realizing its full value will require the industry to move beyond thinking about storage as a single asset class. Different grid challenges require different response times, discharge durations, and operating characteristics, and the storage strategy should reflect those differences.
Why Grid Resilience Requires More Flexibility
The power industry is simultaneously managing rapid load growth and infrastructure that can take years to expand. That mismatch matters. New generation projects do little to relieve a local constraint if the transmission infrastructure needed to move that power is not available. Likewise, adding generating capacity does not necessarily address short periods of extreme demand or provide the rapid response needed when conditions change unexpectedly. Storage creates another option.
Energy storage can help address gaps between when and where power is available and when it is needed. That can include utility-scale storage as well as systems deployed closer to the load.
The latter will become increasingly important as data centers, manufacturing plants, hospitals, and other large energy users invest in more sophisticated on-site power systems. Those resources will primarily serve the reliability needs of the facilities themselves, but where capacity is available, they can also push power back out to the grid to provide another source of flexibility during high-stress periods.
Energy storage isn’t a substitute for investment in generation or transmission; those investments remain essential. However, it can help the industry make better use of existing infrastructure while longer-term projects are developed.
Different Energy Storage Applications Require Different Battery Technologies
As the role of storage expands, the industry also needs to move past the idea that one battery technology will emerge as the universal solution. Grid resilience is not one application.
A system providing instantaneous response or short-duration ride-through is performing a fundamentally different job than a system shifting several hours of renewable generation. A facility maintaining critical operations through a prolonged outage has another set of requirements. Those differences matter when selecting battery technology.
For shorter-duration applications requiring reliable high-power performance, established battery technologies such as advanced lead and lithium can play important roles. As discharge requirements extend, technologies designed for long-duration energy storage, including vanadium redox flow batteries, become increasingly beneficial.
In some cases, the most resilient solution may incorporate more than one battery technology. A hybrid system could use one battery technology for rapid response and another for longer-duration energy needs. Rather than forcing a single chemistry to satisfy every requirement, this technology-agnostic approach allows the storage architecture to be designed around the actual operating profile.
The question should not be which battery chemistry wins. It should be which combination of technologies best addresses the specific reliability and resilience requirements of the application.
Why Domestic Manufacturing and Recycling Matter
A battery system may remain in service for decades. During that time, operators need confidence that replacement components, technical expertise, and service support will remain available. A strong supply chain is therefore essential to the technology’s long-term resilience.
Recent disruptions have demonstrated the risk of depending heavily on globally concentrated supply chains for critical materials and components. For energy storage systems that may ultimately support critical grid and facility operations, domestic manufacturing capacity, access to materials, and established recycling infrastructure can reduce another source of uncertainty.
Recycling is particularly important because it can create a domestic source of materials for future battery production rather than leaving the industry entirely dependent on newly mined or imported resources.
The lead battery industry provides one established example of that model, with a mature domestic recycling network that recovers materials from end-of-life batteries and returns them to manufacturing. As newer battery technologies scale, developing similarly robust circular supply chains should be part of the industry’s long-term resilience strategy.
Building Resilience Around More Options
The grid challenges emerging today will not be solved by a single technology. The U.S. will need additional generation, expanded transmission and distribution infrastructure, and continued grid modernization. Large energy users will also need to take a more active role in managing their own power requirements. Energy storage can help connect those efforts by giving the system more options when conditions change.
A resilient grid is ultimately one that can adapt. Building more flexibility into the system across technologies, durations, and locations will give grid operators and energy users more ways to respond.
— Scott Childers is vice president, Industry & Technology, with Stryten Energy .

With the trucking sector anticipating the release of the final rule by the Environmental Protection Agency on nitrogen oxide (NoX) standards–known colloquially as EPA ‘27–and what engines need to do to get there, one of the country’s biggest truck retailers took the issue head on its recent earnings call with analysts.
The message by William Rush, the CEO of Rush Enterprises (NASDAQ: RUSHA) and known through the industry as Rusty, was that the final rule may not be coming down anytime soon.
Rush said on the company’s earnings call with analysts Wednesday that “I’m hearing we’re not going to get it in November,” “it” being a final EPA decision following its July Notice of Proposed Rulemaking covering potential amendments to the earlier rule on NoX emissions from heavy-duty vehicles.
The initial proposed regulation and its amendments have numerous parts. But at the core, it will require about an 80% reduction in NoX emissions to get down to 0.035 g/bhp-hr, which represents grams of pollutant per brake horsepower-hour. There is no change in that basic part of the proposal.
“There have been some things that have gone in the EPA that are going to delay it,” Rush said, without offering specifics. “Possibly we’re going to be told to just work off a draft.”
EPA ‘27’s name is a reference to the model year engines where the tighter NoX rules will need to be met. And a truck retailer like Rush is going to be on the front end of whatever decisions are made by OEMs in how to meet the broader rule that is in place, either with some regulations that OEMs and others have not challenged, like the actual NoX limits, but others that are the subject of industry criticism, such as changes in warranty length.
Rush’s prediction in the earnings call: “We’ll get the final decree out in January or February, but it’s got to go on the first of January,” he said. “So it’s kind of up in the air exactly what is really going to stay the same.”
Wide backing for NCPs
The provision in the July amendments that garnered the most industry support were the noncompliance penalties (NCPs) that engine manufacturers can pay should they fail to meet the new standards. However, the NCPs are not a permanent change and will phase out.
Rush, from his perspective, is looking at OEMs that supply his retail outlets delivering NoX compliant or non-compliant vehicles on differing schedules, should the NCPs be adopted as an amendment to the original rule. “I’ve never seen an EPA law or decree where it wasn’t the same for everybody on one particular date ,” Rush told the analysts. “Some will come in on January 1. Some may not do it until the following year.”
However, Rush added that “I don’t believe we’ve had time to truly test these engines.”
“So I think from a customer perspective, I would be leaning towards wanting to pay some NCPs, that’s my personal opinion, and roll in and test the new technology before I go all into the pool,” Rush said. “Let’s dive into the shallow end, not the deep end.”
‘Expiditiously’ at EPA
In a prepared statement sent to FreightWaves, a spokesman for EPA said the agency “recognizes the importance of timely action to provide regulatory certainty for manufacturers and the trucking industry. The agency is carefully reviewing the comments received and is working to finalize the rule as expeditiously as possible.”
Rush cited several OEMs by name, saying they were in favor of the NCPs. And their comments made to the EPA during the comment period on the amendments back that up.
For example, PACCAR (NASDAQ: PCAR) , which Rush mentioned, said in its comments to EPA that it “strongly supports EPA’s proposal to establish nonconformance penalties for medium and heavy-heavy duty engines for the NOx standard.”
“The 2027 NOx standards meet the Clean Air Act’s criteria for nonconformance penalties, and they are critical to ensuring industry launches with robust and fully validated products rather than accelerating products to market before validation is complete,” PACCAR said in its comments.
Rush also mentioned engine manufacturer Cummins (NYSE: CMI).
Cummins, in its submission from late August, requested the EPA move quickly on the amendments, something Rush’s comments suggest is not going to occur.
“There is an urgent need for EPA to finalize some of the proposed amendments as soon as possible, for example, those related to emissions warranty, emissions useful life, and nonconformance penalties, so EPA can certify manufacturers’ model year 2027 engines to the revised provisions and manufacturers can introduce them into commerce by January 1, 2027,” Cummins said.
The reference by Cummins to other provisions under study by EPA include the questions of warranty and useful life, which are somewhat similar.
Warranty and useful life provisions
As Rush Truck Centers described it in their own Q&A on the EPA ‘27 rules , useful life “is a regulatory requirement that determines how long an engine must continue meeting federal emissions standards for certification purposes.”
As Rush Truck Centers added, the proposed amendment would not implement tighter useful-life standards until 2030, giving a three-year breather.
The warranty changes in the amendment would keep current requirements in place rather than the original changes, which would have forced OEMs to recognize longer warranties. It has been noted by several of the commenters on the amendments that this change alone is expected to have the greatest financial impact on restraining increases on the price of the cleaner trucks created by the EPA ‘27 rule.
Warranty table is from Rush Enterprises’ web page
Rush on the earnings call referred to the EPA sarcastically as “our great government that can’t seem to write a final decree.” But he softened that by saying that “I know there are a lot of legal ramifications. They have to be very careful with the changes. They have tried to make it easier for the customers.”
The NCPs, Rush said, will allow greater testing of the tighter NoX engines without actually adopting them in fleets.
“Most folks want to run this stuff for over a year before they roll it into their fleets, because we’ve seen through history that new technology does not always run right out of the gate,” Rush said.
The rollout of diesel exhaust fluid (DEF) in 2010, Rush said as an example, resulted in “clogged particulate filters all over the country.”
DEF gets some changes in the proposed amendments. Despite some online misinterpretation that the rule for diesel engines to use DEF is disappearing, what would change in the amendments would be the elimination of the “deratement,” where low DEF levels result in engines slowing the vehicle they are powering. Instead, audio alerts would replace them.
ATA reiterates NCP backing
In a coincidence, the American Trucking Associations had already made its views on the proposed amendments known during the comment period , but about the same time Rush was making its comments, the ATA used the group’s blog last week to reiterate its view on the changes in EPA ‘27.
The blog post was put up by ATA, according to a spokesman, “because the rule is up for interagency review in the coming weeks and it reiterates our stance on the rule. Congress left town, but this is content that speaks to important activity happening at the agencies.”
Like the OEMs made clear in their own comments, the ATA favors the NCPs as a key transition tool.
ATA said of the changes in general that they “lay out a responsible path forward, maintaining ambitious NOx emissions reduction targets while recognizing that manufacturers need sufficient time to test new technologies under real-world operating conditions.”
“NCPs preserve the incentive for manufacturers to meet the new standard as quickly as possible while preventing reliable engine models from becoming unavailable in the market,” the ATA said. “As EPA prepares to finalize its rulemaking, the NCP provisions must remain intact. Without them, the rule would lose a critical safeguard for truck availability, fleet reliability, and an orderly transition to the next generation of emissions technology.”

Debtor-in-process financing up to $55 million could keep the lights on at Karyopharm Therapeutics for its multiple myeloma and myelofibrosis programs as the biotech waits to see if its union with Ayrmid will go through.
Less than three months after revealing significant financial strain, Karyopharm Therapeutics has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy as it works toward a merger with U.K. biotech Ayrmid.
The commercial-stage companies’ transaction is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027, according to the Monday announcement , which came in lieu of expected third quarter earnings from Karyopharm.
During the transaction process, the biopharma will remain focused on its commitment to advancing its multiple myeloma and myelofibrosis programs and will “operate in the ordinary course of business,” Karyopharm noted.
Ayrmid, which is developing therapies that address significant unmet needs in hematology, is serving as lead bidder in the court-supervised sale of Karyopharm, which markets the multiple myeloma drug Xpovio and has a pipeline of clinical candidates. Other companies can still submit competing proposals and bids for the biopharma’s assets.
Monday’s announcement was not wholly unexpected, as Karyopharm reported in August that it only had enough cash to carry on into September.
The companies have not disclosed the amount of Ayrmid’s bid, but Karyopharm did reveal that it had secured commitments for up to $55 million in debtor-in-process financing from its existing secured lenders. Once approved by the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of Texas, that money, along with cash generated from the company’s ongoing operations, is expected to support the biopharma during the Chapter 11 process.
News of the filing and planned merger failed to garner strong support from Rodman & Renshaw. In a Monday note, the investment firm downgraded its outlook of Karyopharm, explaining that lenders and note holders will recover equity first, leaving the value left for shareholders highly uncertain—it “could be minimal,” the analysts wrote.
“Our estimates, scenarios, and price target were built on an operating-company framework,” the analysts continued. “That framework assumed the equity would capture the value of the commercial and pipeline assets, and it no longer fits.”
The firm had previously put Karyopharm at a $986.6 million enterprise value and a $15 per share intrinsic value.
As Karyopharm works to stay afloat, its future workforce structure remains somewhat up in the air. But it may not mean the end of the road for the biopharma’s workforce.
“There are no layoffs associated with today’s announcement of the planned merger,” a spokesperson at FTI Consulting, Karyopharm’s financial and communications advisor, told BioSpace in an email. “While it is too early to say what may ultimately come from the transaction, we understand from Ayrmid that they intend to retain the majority of Karyopharm’s organization, recognizing the valuable capabilities that exist within the team.”
Recent business challenges
Karyopharm previously announced workforce cuts in August 2023, August 2024 and July 2025, as noted in an SEC filing earlier this year. The most recent downsizing, in July 2025, involved letting go of 20% of staff to help manage operating expenses. At that time, the company was exploring its options to extend its cash runway, which it noted could include a merger or sale.
In Karyopharm’s Monday announcement, Joe Wiley, Ayrmid chairman and CEO, noted a strong strategic fit between the two companies given their complementary portfolios, established commercial capabilities and shared commitment to addressing significant unmet needs in hematology.
Karyopharm’s only marketed product, Xpovio, has been approved for the treatment of relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma, a rare blood cancer in which abnormal plasma cells multiply and produce abnormal proteins that can affect bones, kidneys and blood cells.
The company has also been advancing Xpovio for another rare blood cancer, myelofibrosis, in which scar tissue forms in bone marrow and leads to conditions including anemia and an enlarged spleen. In March, the company announced mixed results in a Phase 3 myelofibrosis study, with an investigational Xpovio regimen meeting just one of two primary endpoints. A few months later, however, Karyopharm submitted a supplemental new drug application to the FDA requesting accelerated approval for the indication, in combination with Incyte’s Jakafi.
Ayrmid has two FDA-approved products, Omisirge and Aphexda. Omisirge is used for the treatment of blood cancers in adults and children ages 12 years and older and severe aplastic anemia in adults and children six years and older. Aplastic anemia is a rare blood disorder that occurs when there aren’t enough blood cells and platelets in the body. Aphexda is used to mobilize hematopoietic stem cells in adult patients with multiple myeloma.

Car Nut Takes Anemic U-Code 1970 Challenger to the Dyno, Goes Home With Hemi-Slaying Performance
20 photos
Photo: YouTube/ValigruntPerformance
Detroit’s finest were great and all, but American muscle of the sixties and seventies didn’t have a real following outside the United States of Automobile. With one notable exception: Australia, the country where roads are longer, lonelier, and more inviting than even those from the Land of the Free. Three reasons for which a 1970 Challenger R/T 440-4 needed an urgent repair to its damaged muscle reputation.
The first-generation Dodge Challenger R/T debuted on September 25, 1969, for the 1970 model year. It brought forth something no other pony car before had dared to (with the notable exception of the E-body Barracuda, of course): the biggest displacement engine, the 440 Magnum.
It was a boulevard bruiser of cataclysmic proportions back then, and one of those ruffians went in for a health check and a dyno run. When an orange 1970 Dodge Challenger R/T hardtop wearing Victorian registration plates DODG 00 rolled into the Dandenong South workshop of Australian Mopar specialist Shane Withers, it looked every bit the classic American ruffian.
Yet, as documented on the Valigrunt Performance YouTube channel, the coupe suffered from an embarrassing lack of testosterone, prompting Withers and co-host Kylie Withers to joke that the big-block machine performed like a two-cylinder Daihatsu.
Photo: YouTube/ValigruntPerformance That lethargy stood in stark contrast to the fearsome reputation of the Chrysler 440-cubic-inch RB (raised block) eight-cylinder. Manufactured by Chrysler from 1966 through 1978 with a 4.32-inch bore and a 3.75-inch stroke, the 7.2-liter engine was offered in the first-generation Dodge Challenger exclusively during the 1970 and 1971 model years, before punitive insurance surcharges and tightening federal emissions standards banished big-block power from the E-body pony car.
Across those two model years, Dodge assembled 6,125 total 440-powered Challengers out of 165,437 first-generation cars built between 1970 and 1974. The 1970 debut accounted for 5,875 big-block 440 examples, reserved strictly for the performance-oriented R/T series. By 1971, Dodge canceled the four-barrel 440 option for the United States market, building just 250 V-code 440 Six-Pack R/T hardtops worldwide, including 246 domestic cars split into 127 4-speed manuals and 119 3-speed automatics.
Photo: YouTube/ValigruntPerformance During the 1970 model year, buyers choosing the 440-cubic-inch V8 had two catalog options. The U-code 440 Magnum breathed through a single Carter AVS four-barrel carburetor atop a 9.7:1 compression ratio, generating 375 hp, or 380 PS, at 4,600 rpm and 480 lb-ft, or 651 Nm, of torque at 3,200 rpm, pushing a tested Challenger from 0 to 60 mph in 5.8 seconds and through the quarter-mile in 14.1 seconds.
Dodge produced 3,840 U-code 440 Magnum Challengers in 1970 across three R/T body styles. Standard R/T two-door hardtops accounted for 2,802 cars, divided between 1,886 3-speed TorqueFlite automatics and 916 Pistol Grip A833 4-speed manuals. Another 875 customers ordered the luxurious R/T Special Edition hardtop, comprising 733 TorqueFlite automatics and 142 manuals, while the open-air R/T convertible saw just 163 U-code builds (129 automatics).
The V-code 440 Six-Pack added a 10.5:1 compression ratio and three Holley two-barrel carburetors, delivering 390 hp, or 395 PS, at 4,700 rpm, 490 lb-ft, or 664 Nm, at 3,200 rpm, and a 13.7-second quarter-mile at 105 mph. Dodge built 2,035 units in 1970: 1,640 R/T hardtops with 793 automatics and 847 manuals, 296 Special Editions with 161 automatics and 135 manuals, and 99 convertibles with 38 automatics and 61 row-your-own 4-speeds.
Photo: YouTube/ValigruntPerformance Unfortunately, the orange 1970 Challenger R/T hardtop inspected by Shane Withers no longer carried a high-compression 1970 Magnum powerplant. Beneath its dual-scoop hood sat a low-compression replacement 440-cubic-inch V8 coupled to a New Process A833 4-speed manual gearbox and cast-iron exhaust manifolds. Strapped onto a rolling chassis dynamometer upon arrival, the Challenger mustered a pavement-pounding 232 rear-wheel hp (235 PS), alongside 467 lb-ft, or 633 Nm, of torque.
Tasked with waking up the big-block Mopar without pulling the short block from the engine bay, Withers unbolted the cylinder heads and immediately saw why the motor was wheezing. The pistons sat a staggering 0.100 inch, or 2.54 mm, below the deck surface, resulting in an ultra-low static compression ratio better suited to burning kerosene than premium gasoline. Leaving the bottom end untouched, Withers devised a top-end recipe to salvage the lazy 440.
To claw back lost cylinder pressure, Valigrunt Performance bolted on a pair of CNC-ported 440 Source aluminum cylinder heads featuring smaller combustion chambers, mated to thin Cometic head gaskets that raised the static compression ratio to 8.9:1. Withers then installed 1.7:1 ratio roller rockers to increase valve lift across the existing camshaft profile, topped the block with an Edelbrock Performer Air-Gap aluminum intake manifold, and dropped in an MSD Ready-to-Run electronic distributor.
Photo: YouTube/ValigruntPerformance Out on an initial road test, the revitalized 440 spun the rear tires effortlessly in first gear, but grabbing second gear exposed a glaring drivetrain weakness as the clutch slipped violently. Pulling the 4-speed transmission revealed a Borg and Beck clutch whose pressure plate had overheated and warped into a concave cup, showing daylight along its inner friction surface. Withers installed a McLeod clutch assembly and mounted the Challenger onto his Mainline hub dynamometer.
Even the new McLeod unit slipped during the opening pulls, prompting Withers to bed the disc in on the hubs by shifting aggressively through the gears until it locked solidly by run 6. After verifying the air-fuel mixture and backing initial ignition timing down from its arrival setting of 15 degrees to 10 degrees, the 440 immediately hammered out 405.3 hp (411 PS), and 550 lb-ft (746 Nm).
Testing 12 degrees of initial timing cost power, so Withers dialed in 7 degrees and fitted lighter distributor advance springs to cure a low-rpm flat spot. Back-to-back final pulls yielded 412.1 rear-wheel hp (418 PS), and 551.7 lb-ft (748 Nm)—a gain of 180.1 hp and 84.7 lb-ft. An upgraded power-steering box and swapped front tires completed the transformation, leaving only a pair of mismatched-batch Vietnamese twin fan belts screeching under load.

Tesla has launched Heat Pump Optimization, a feature that lets the Powerwall 3 and three-phase Powerwall 3P tell a compatible heat pump when to run harder so a home can bank cheap or surplus solar energy as hot water.
It’s live in Europe only. Tesla hasn’t said anything about bringing it to the US or Canada, and the hardware standard it relies on barely exists on this side of the Atlantic.
How Tesla’s Heat Pump Optimization works
According to Tesla’s support page for the feature , the Powerwall watches electricity prices and solar production throughout the day and sends the heat pump one of two signals: run normally, or boost.
When it’s told to boost, the heat pump heats water beyond what the home needs right now, typically into a domestic hot water or buffer tank. That stored heat then carries the house through the expensive hours, when the heat pump can run less.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
What triggers a boost depends on the Powerwall’s operating mode:
In Self-Powered mode, it boosts only when there’s surplus solar left after the home’s other loads are covered.
In Savings mode, it boosts when solar is available or when grid power hits its cheapest price, based on 24-hour tariff forecasts.
Tesla Energy summed it up on X last week: “Heat Pump Optimization allows your Powerwall to boost heating when there’s surplus solar or energy is inexpensive.”
The SG-Ready catch
There’s no cloud integration with heat pump brands here. It’s a wire.
The feature runs on SG-Ready (Smart Grid Ready), a label the German Heat Pump Association (BWP) introduced back in 2012 with 17 manufacturers. It uses two relay contacts on the heat pump to signal four operating states, from a utility block to a forced switch-on. Tesla only uses the “normal” and “boosted” recommendations.
Tesla’s requirements are pretty specific:
Powerwall 3 or Powerwall 3P on firmware 26.26 or later
An SG-Ready-certified heat pump with an accessible SG-2 contact, configured to accept external signals
Physical wiring between the Powerwall and the heat pump, installed and commissioned by a Tesla-certified installer
Tesla app version 4.59.1 or later
And there are limits. The signals are only recommendations, so the heat pump’s own thermostat settings can override them. Tesla also notes each signal has to be held for at least 10 minutes to comply with SG-Ready, and the feature drops back to normal during a power outage so the Powerwall can prioritize backup loads.
Oddly, there’s no on/off toggle in the Tesla app. Once it’s wired up, it’s on.
Why a hot water tank is a cheap battery
The math is what makes this interesting. A 300-liter hot water tank heated an extra 30°C holds about 10.5 kWh of thermal energy. With a heat pump running at a COP of 3, that takes only around 3.5 kWh of electricity to store.
So a tank most European heat pump homes already have can soak up a big chunk of midday solar without touching the lithium in the garage. That leaves the Powerwall’s 13.5 kWh free for the stuff that can’t be stored as heat.
The market is there too. Germany sold 299,000 heating heat pumps in 2025, up 55% year-over-year according to BWP, and they made up nearly half of all new heating systems sold in the country for the first time.
Tesla is also late to this. sonnen pushed a software update in 2023 that lets its sonnenBatterie run heat pumps off surplus solar, starting with NIBE units, and SG-Ready control has been a standard feature of German PV energy managers for years.

It’s the latest Europe-first move for Tesla Energy after it launched the Powerwall 3P with a native three-phase inverter earlier this year, aimed squarely at Germany, Austria, and Switzerland. The company announced its 1 millionth Powerwall last year, and software like this is how it squeezes more value out of that installed base.
Electrek’s Take

Networking
Marvell TX9190 Switch At OCP 2025 1
Marvell Technology announced today that it has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire Lumentum in an all-stock transaction with an implied value of about $115 billion. The proposed deal aims to merge Marvell’s electrical interconnect and custom silicon portfolio with Lumentum’s high-performance lasers, optical circuit switching (OCS), and compound semiconductor manufacturing capabilities. For AI infrastructure designers facing the physical limits of copper, this combination could drive deeper co-design across the entire signal chain, from distributed data centers to connections within advanced semiconductor packages.
Bridging the Copper Wall with Integrated Optics
The primary driver for this acquisition is the industry transition from electrical to optical connectivity as AI clusters scale. At the Marvell Computex 2026 Keynote , CEO Matt Murphy described connectivity as the next major bottleneck in data center design, noting that compute performance gains are outpacing connectivity and networking gains. Marvell has positioned itself to address this by offering solutions across various distances, from long-haul coherent links to short-reach scale-up domains. However, the “copper wall,” or the maximum distance copper can viably support before signal integrity fails, is moving closer as lane speeds increase. A copper-to-optics transition is underway in the industry, albeit slower than many people thought it would be 10 years ago.
Marvell’s existing portfolio addresses parts of this challenge with products like the COLORZ 800 module, which we examined in Going 800Gbps at up to 1000km with the Marvell COLORZ 800 . That module uses coherent detection and a local oscillator to maintain signal integrity over vast distances, packaging complex DSPs and photonics into a standard OSFP form factor. While effective for long-reach scale-across links, the move toward co-packaged optics (CPO) requires even tighter integration between the switch silicon and the optical engine.
Marvell Development Board COLORZ III Tabletop Setup Optical Side Angle
The proposed combination pairs Marvell’s electrical and optical interconnect, CMOS/silicon photonics, switching/custom silicon design, and packaging expertise with Lumentum’s specialized compound semiconductor manufacturing, including indium phosphide (InP), plus high-speed and high-power lasers.
As we saw in our Marvell TX9190 CPO switch coverage from OCP 2025 , near-package optical engines shorten the electrical path, with fiber runs and pluggable light sources replacing long PCB traces. We also saw some neat technology on our recent AWS Networking Lab tour .
By acquiring Lumentum, Marvell intends to control more of this supply chain internally and design solutions across a larger domain instead of having to go to different companies for different parts.
Marvell TX9190 Switch At OCP 2025 7
Beyond component integration, Lumentum brings optical circuit switching (OCS) to the combined portfolio. The Lumentum R300 OCS establishes direct optical paths between endpoints using micro-electro-mechanical systems (MEMS) mirrors, eliminating intermediate packet processing and optical-electrical-optical (OEO) conversion along those switched paths. Lumentum says this results in dramatically lower latency, higher signal integrity, and significant reductions in network power for large GPU clusters.
Acquiring Lumentum and its technology will not come cheap, however. The $115 billion deal is being financed entirely with Marvell’s stock, significantly leveraging the value of the roughly $175 billion company in order to pay for the deal. In effect, this makes the deal closer to a merger than a buy-out. Following the settlement of the deal, Marvell shareholders will own 67% of the new company, while Lumentum shareholders will own the other 33%. Similarly, the deal will see three members of Lumentum’s board of directors join Marvell’s board, bringing it up to 10 members.
Final Words
This deal, expected to close in the first half of 2028, so some time away, coordinates Marvell electrical and optical interconnect plus silicon design with Lumentum lasers, optical manufacturing, and OCS. The companies intend closer co-design and optimized, pre-validated optical solutions, faster time to market, and high-volume production, but that close is a long way away. This is a huge deal when companies are seeing valuations soar due to AI demand.

The newest module in Supply Chain Intelligence: Custom Insights uses a shipper’s own freight data to flag lanes that could move from truckload to intermodal , or between spot and contract, and estimates the savings lane by lane.
SONAR has added mode conversion optimization to SCI: Custom Insights, part of its Supply Chain Intelligence (SCI) platform, with Conversion Optimization. The new module uses a shipper’s own network data to show where freight can convert between over-the-road truckload and intermodal, and between spot and contract, and estimates the savings on each lane. Shippers can adjust the volume they want to test, and SCI recalculates total estimated savings across every selected lane.
The Conversion optimization view in SCI: Custom Insights, with tabs for truckload to intermodal, spot to contract and contract to spot.
At a glance
What it is: a mode and pricing-strategy optimizer inside SCI: Custom Insights
What it finds: lanes ready for truckload-to-intermodal, spot-to-contract or contract-to-spot conversion
What it calculates: estimated savings per lane and in total, based on the volume you choose to convert
Who it’s for: procurement, network planning and finance teams at shippers in the SONAR Shipper Consortium
Released: October 2026
What is SCI Conversion optimization?
Conversion optimization is a module within SCI: Custom Insights, the consortium-powered experience in SONAR Supply Chain Intelligence. It shows shippers where they can convert between over-the-road truckload and intermodal, and between spot and contract, to reduce transportation costs, using their own freight data and SONAR market benchmarks.
It covers both conversions in three views:
Over-the-r oad to intermodal: lanes where rail intermodal can carry the freight for less than over-the-road truckload
Spot to contract: lanes where freight repeatedly lands on the spot market and a contract rate would be cheaper and steadier
Contract to spot: lanes where contracted rates sit above the spot market and moving volume to spot would save money
How does Conversion optimization work?
Three conversion views: separate tabs for truckload to intermodal, spot to contract and contract to spot
Side-by-side rates: each lane shows the shipper’s current rate next to SONAR intermodal contract, truckload contract and truckload spot rates
Terminal distance: truckload-to-intermodal lanes show miles to the nearest rail terminal
Estimated savings: shown per lane in dollars and as a cost-per-load savings percentage, plus a total across all selected lanes
Adjustable volume: change the volume on any lane to match planned changes, and total savings recalculate automatically
Filters and export: set a date range, select lanes and export the data for bid planning and rate reviews
The volume control matters. Few shippers will move 100% of a lane to intermodal overnight. Testing 20%, 40% or 60% shows the savings at each level, so teams can build a realistic conversion plan.
Why mode decisions matter right now
The gap between intermodal and truckload contract rates shifts with the market, and so does the gap between spot and contract pricing. When over-the-road contract rates climb faster than intermodal, conversion savings grow. [STAT: current intermodal vs. van contract savings from SONAR]
Most shippers make these calls once a year, during the RFP. Conversion optimization lets them revisit the decision whenever the market moves, not just at bid time.
How it fits into the SCI platform
Conversion optimization is the newest module in SCI: Custom Insights, which launched in September 2026. It builds on:
Custom Insights’ network view , which pairs a shipper’s own data from the SONAR Shipper Consortium with market benchmarks to track network health
Redesigned SCI experience with a Risk and Efficiency Quadrant for faster RFP guidance
Manual Analysis , the original SCI workflow, still available for mini-bids, project freight and new lanes
New contract-based datasets released alongside Conversion optimization: Routing Guide Premium (RGP), Routing Guide Acceptance Share (RGAS) and Contract Rate Change Direction (CRCD)
Together, they move SCI from showing where a shipper is overpaying to showing what to do about it.
Who should use it
Procurement teams planning RFPs, mini-bids or mid-cycle rate reviews
Network planners weighing intermodal for long-haul, high-volume lanes
Finance leaders forecasting transportation spend and looking for savings
Logistics managers with lanes that keep falling to the spot market
How to get started
SCI: Custom Insights users can log in to SONAR and open Conversion optimization within Custom Insights. Shippers not yet in the Shipper Consortium can ask their account manager about contributing data. For a walkthrough, contact your SONAR account manager. Shippers new to SONAR can request a demo .
FAQs:
What is SONAR SCI Conversion optimization? It is a module in SCI: Custom Insights, part of SONAR Supply Chain Intelligence, that finds lanes where a shipper could save money by converting between over-the-road truckload and intermodal, or between spot and contract, and estimates the savings.
Which mode conversions does SONAR SCI evaluate? Two: between over-the-road truckload and intermodal, and between spot and contract (in both directions).
Can I test converting only part of a lane’s volume? Yes. Users set the volume they want to evaluate on each lane, and SCI recalculates total estimated savings across all selected lanes.
How does Conversion optimization fit into SCI: Custom Insights? It is a module inside Custom Insights. Custom Insights pairs a shipper’s own data with SONAR benchmarks to show network health, and Conversion optimization uses that same data to recommend mode and pricing-strategy changes by lane.
When should shippers consider truckload-to-intermodal conversion? Usually on long-haul, high-volume lanes with flexible transit times, especially when truckload contract rates rise faster than intermodal rates.
How do I access Conversion optimization? Shippers using SCI: Custom Insights can find it inside Custom Insights in SONAR. New users can request a demo or learn more about SONAR at gosonar.com.

11 New Hot Wheels to Make You Happy Next Year
37 photos
Photo: Lamley Group
I know I say this all the time, but the rate a which Mattel creates new Hot Wheels is astonishing. I’m trying to keep up with every new release and preview, while also looking at the brand’s history. And it can often get tricky to be in touch with everything.
For instance, just last night I was writing about the latest development for Mattel Brick Shop. Downsizing to 1/64th-scale models should help solve the price issue, which has likely kept many enthusiasts away. It looks like a brilliant idea to me and I plan on buying a few of them once they’re available in my area. The thing is that while I was writing about the new Racer Series , I discovered a preview of some new items for 2027.
It seems Mr. Lambert still has some content from last month’s 40th Annual Hot Wheels Collectors Convention in Los Angeles. Hot Wheels designers Rob Matthes and Kristina Albrecht were at the scene talking about the upcoming Racing Culture line and Team Transport . Phil Riehlman and Mario Godoy showed us the news for Elite 64. Then, Ronald Wong walked us through the Premium updates.
For the latest preview we’ve got Bryan Zhao and Thomas Kim showing off some Basic models plus some cars with Real Riders wheels that I did not see coming. Thomas has only been working for Mattel for a short while, which means 2027 marks his debut with three new castings. One of them happens to be the 1999 Toyota MR-S we’ve seen before. It’s coming to the Premium Fast and Furious series next year, and the fun part is that he actually owns of these in the real world.
As for Bryan Zhao, the Rink Racer was one of his first Hot Wheels designs back in 2024, and he has worked on many Tooned and original castings since. The BMW 635 Csi, the McMurtry Spéirling, the BMW M4 GT3 and Terra Torque are his hottest ones yet, and he seems to be ready for a few more in 2027. Some of the cars in the first part of the video have been leaked before, which is why I only focused on the ones I’ve personally never seen before.
Shelby has entered the chat Photo: Lamley Group I did include a photo of the Braille Racer Deora though, for that close-up shot on the turntable. I can instantly tell that the '25 Shelby F-150 Super Snake is going to simply fly off the pegs when it comes out. I typically prefer older pickup trucks to what’s available on the market right now, but this thing is in a league of its own.
The Atlas Blue finish with white stripes, the stance, and even the wheels all add up for one hot collectible, and I imagine people would lose their minds if his ever reached Super Treasure Hunt status. This would have worked nicely in Team Transport, too, and by the end of this story you’ll see the team had something similar in mind for that series. The moment I saw Thomas Kim’s Starting Block, I immediately thought of the recent Porsche 908-3.
I know one of my Hot Wheels dealers is a big fan of these wooden-style vehicles, and it certainly seems that Mattel is planning on expanding the line-up. I’d say Starting Bloc is one of the nicer releases in the line, alongside the Chop’n Bloc and Bloc Aid (Track Fleet). The proposition is still not interesting enough for me, and I’d honestly rather go after the Cosmic Shifter instead.
Fraser Campbell created this concept, and you could say it’s partially a tribute to Ira Gilford’s late ‘60s Twin Mill as the front end look similar. It almost feels like a flying saucer landed on that casting to create this hybrid. I like the contrast between the ZAMAC-like chrome finish, the purple flames and Aerodisc wheels and the green base. I can assure you that most (if not all) of the Hot Wheels original casting feature clever design cues that reveal the story behind the idea.
At last, a Hot Wheels with a functional suspension setup Photo: Lamley Group And it’s part of why following this hobby is so fun in the first place. I’ve been aiming to buy an RC buggy for years now, but other priorities have always gotten in the way. My wife wanted to surprise me after my Michelin/Porsche 911 GT3 RS test last year and got me a battery powered replica of Zuffenhausen’s flagship sportscar. But there’s no way I can enjoy it out here in the countryside, where a buggy or a Monster Truck would reign supreme.
I’ve never had the pleasure to play with a Tyco Jet Hopper before, and seeing Charlie Angulo’s Hot Wheels version of the iconic RC car makes me want one badly. I almost fell off my chair when I realized this casting features a working suspension, something that I’m used to seeing over at Tomica for instance. I’d say it’s the next best feature after having moving or removable parts, but it can go the other way around, too.
I can see this model becoming a big hit with collectors worldwide, and it’s probably safe to say we’ll see at least one other variation showing up in stores before 2028. The trend of paying tribute to oldschool toys continues with the Corn Shaker and my only complaint is that I know it won’t fit into my Kruzzel transport case. I guess it’s meant to be enjoyed and not tucked away to never be seen again.
There’s obviously no shortage of ‘80s rally cars that don’t have a Hot Wheels equivalent yet, but I don’t mind seeing the fictional Turbo Crest here. We already have plenty of options in the Premium series, and I think I partly regret letting go of my RLC 1985 Audi Sport quattro S1 (I won’t be selling the Porsche 959 though!). Turbo Crest is the same kind of mashup we’ve witnessed with the Hako Type D.
That’s a huge wing! Photo: Lamley Group Maybe it’ll look nicer once it gets an actual livery as it’s still too early to tell if it’s going anywhere at this stage. The 1950s themed Pickup Gasser could bring in a wave of fans from the ‘55 Bel Air Gasser and other similar collectibles. The StepAside warning on the tailgate is a cool touch, and it reminds me that Mattel still “owes” us another Dragstrip Demons set in Car Culture. I have mixed feelings about the next car on the list.
I guess we were all hoping to see the C8 ZR1 as soon as possible, but I just didn’t think the convertible version would come first. Maybe Mattel is saving the Coupe for a premium-exclusive release, which is fine by me. While I normally enjoy Aerodisc wheels, I wouldn’t use them for this car. The PR5 rims we saw on Phil Riehlman’s entry-level C8 were much nicer and that raises the question: why haven’t we gotten a new variation for that casting since 2024?
Anyway, I’ve started paying more attention to Mattel’s Track Fleet series in recent years, as it seems like a more affordable, yet still fun version of Team Transport. I’ve never played golf in my life and it’s not a sport I’m itching to try, but you have to admit that Birdie Burner is a cool project! It’s one of two new castings in Track Fleet’s Mix 1 for 2027, alongside the Drag Camaro I’ve already shown you a little while ago.
Playing mini-golf using a Hot Wheels trailer wasn’t something I expected would happen in 2027. I’m not nearly as enthusiastic about the next premium Toyota 4Runner casting (TRD Pro version), and it might be due to the fact that I’ve never experienced one in the real world.
Well, it’s not like I’ve ever driven a GMC Sierra 3500 either, but there are several elements to observe here: the dually setup and the new trailer! The only question is: what kind of vehicle will it be transporting? We should find out within the next few months!

Coachbuilt 1938 Lincoln Has 57 Years With One Family, Jay Leno Can't Have Enough of Its 414-Cube V12
73 photos
Photo: YouTube/Jay Leno's Garage
“It’s not the cleanest car that we brought to you, but that’s because we really do like to drive this thing.” No, it’s not a pickup truck. And it’s not a minivan, dad wagon, or SUV, either. It has zero electronic components in. The rear window is smaller than some modern cars’ main infotaintment screens. It only makes 150 horsepower. From a V12. A 6.7-liter V12 with aluminum heads. It’s a Judkins Touring Coupe.
A what? A Lincoln. A 1938 luxury car back from when Detroit (by which I mean America itself) was swarming with so many carmakers, there seemed to be one for every state of the Union. Little by little, they all went down in history, leaving only corporate giants to roam the landscapes. But even those corporate juggernauts started out from one company. Well, maybe except Ford.
Henry Ford established Henry Ford Company at the dawn of the 20th century, in 1901, only to be ousted by investors, who brought in Henry Leland as a consulting engineer to oversee production. Ford stormed out of his own company, taking only the right to the name, leaving Leland and the rest of the bunch with everything else. They made that “everything else” into Cadillac.
With the help of the Dodge bros, Ford established Ford Motor Company in 1903. By the time America got into WWI, in 1917, Leland got busy with the war effort (his expertise as an arms manufacturer helped), and started building aircraft engines. His enterprise was Lincoln Motor Company, and that name couldn’t have been more literal: it was building motors. That was it. After the war, however, with demanding plummeting, Lincoln turned to fine cars.
Photo: YouTube/Jay Leno's Garage By 1922, it went into receivership. Care to guess who put $8 million on the table? Yes, Henry Ford I. His success with the Model T had made FoMoCo into the biggest carmaker in the world, and revenge couldn’t have been sweeter. Edsel Ford was put in charge of Lincoln, and pretty soon, the company put Cadillac squarely in its iron sights. And Packard, Duesenberg, Cord, and every other luxury carmaker from Detroit.
However, Lincoln had something most of its competitors didn’t: a lot of cash from Ford’s unstoppable success with the modest Model Ts and As. As such, Lincoln could afford a lot more operational overhead. Which didn’t stop it from experimenting with coachbuilding, just to one-up its rivals. Enter J.B. Judkins, a long-standing coach builder (as in, it build horse-drawn coaches) established in 1857.
The first Lincoln bodies by Judkins rolled out in 1921. The last one, in 1938. This one, the Touring Coupe Jay Leno drives in the video embedded at the bottom of this story. Cameron Richards, curator of the Nethercutt Collection in Sylmar, California, brought the magnificent one-off for a spin.
Photo: YouTube/Jay Leno's Garage And there’s nothing screaming more late-30s extravaganza that this automotive masterpiece. The automobile is a 1938 Lincoln Model K V12 Touring Coupe, known in period documents as the Judkins Model 1440 or Coupe De Voyage.
Led by president John B. Judkins during the 1920s and 1930s, the company crafted custom bodies for Lincoln, Duesenberg, Packard, and Pierce-Arrow, including 27 Duesenberg bodies and 12 bespoke Model K Lincolns. Although the Great Depression crippled custom coachbuilders, Judkins built 2 final bodies in 1938, thus ending a series of some 5,900 Lincoln shells bearing his company’s signature produced during their partnership.
John B. Judkins constructed this 1938 Lincoln Model K Touring Coupe on speculation specifically for Edsel Ford, president of Ford Motor Company and patron of the Lincoln division. Judkins hoped the bold design would win a limited production contract from Dearborn. Styled by Roland L. Stickney with engineering drafts completed by John F. Dobben and Herman A. Kapp, the fastback silhouette drew direct aesthetic inspiration from a French 1938 Delage.
Photo: YouTube/Jay Leno's Garage When Judkins presented the completed car to Dearborn in 1938, Ford Motor Company stylists rejected the proposal, declaring the automobile far too radical, and ahead of its time. Corporate designers believed conservative buyers would never embrace such an unconventional fastback profile. Ironically, the sweeping roofline and pillarless side glass layout anticipated the hardtop coupe phenomenon that transformed Detroit automobile styling 11 years later during the 1949 season.
As for that swooping , swooning back, we needn’t say a single extra word – we all know how that fashion turned out in the sixties. And, if we take a closer look at what’s going on now, it hasn’t gone out of style even after 90 years.
Hand-hammered from lightweight aluminum panels over an ash wood framework, the Tarragon Green coachwork features a lighter green pinstripe and black fenders. Although configured as a two-door touring coupe, the spacious cabin accommodates five adult passengers. Entry is granted by five-foot-long (1.52-meter) rear-hinged doors whose high-ratio regulators raise the heavy glass in fewer than 3 turns, while the rear quarter windows slide horizontally backward into the aluminum body quarters.
Photo: YouTube/Jay Leno's Garage The expression “big as barn doors” is often used as a hyperbole for something unusually large, but in this case, the barn doors could use the Judkins design as a yardstick for size. Just look at those things – they’re downright enormous!
When Ford Motor Company declined the Coupe De Voyage, John B. Judkins kept the $7,000 showpiece as his personal car. Even after leaving his Merrimac plant in December 1941 before it closed in 1942, Judkins drove the Lincoln until selling it in 1946. While vacationing in Florida during the mid-1960s, Judkins tracked down the owner, bought his beloved final masterpiece back, and drove the car until his passing in 1969.
His widow Elizabeth Judkins contacted family friends J.B. Nethercutt and Dorothy Nethercutt, offering them the cherished automobile. The Nethercutt Collection acquired the Lincoln in 1969, repainted the aluminum body in its original Tarragon Green, and preserved its mechanical configuration. Over the next 57 years, the Nethercutt family drove the car more than 50,000 miles (80,467 kilometers) on tours and picnics.
Photo: YouTube/Jay Leno's Garage To appreciate why John B. Judkins selected the Lincoln Model K as the foundation for his final automotive statement, we need to put the flagship moniker under the magnifying glass. Introduced for the 1931 model year to replace the aging Model L, which had recorded 6,362 units for the 1928 model year prior to the Wall Street crash, the Model K represented Dearborn's finest engineering throughout its 1931 to 1940 production run.
Across its 10 model years from 1931 to 1940, Lincoln manufactured 15,765 examples of the K-series family. Production began with 3,573 V8-powered Model K cars in 1931 before splitting into the 8-cylinder KA and 12-cylinder KB for 1932, yielding 3,647 combined units. Output fell to 1,647 cars in 1933 and 2,411 V12 units in 1934, before unifying under the Model K V12 banner with 1,429 built in 1935 and 1,534 in 1936.
As the streamlined Lincoln-Zephyr captured showroom traffic, Model K V12 volume declined to 977 automobiles in 1937, 416 units for the 1938 model year, 133 cars in 1939, and 18 final deliveries in 1940. For 1938, the standard Model K rested on either a 136-inch (3,454-millimeter) or 145-inch (3,683-millimeter) wheelbase, measuring 210 inches (5,334 millimeters) in length and 63.3 inches (1,608 millimeters) in height, with weights between 5,230 and 5,800 pounds (2,372 and 2,631 kilograms).
Photo: YouTube/Jay Leno's Garage Beneath the long hood of the 1938 Lincoln Model K sat a 67-degree, L-head V12 engine displacing 414 cubic inches (6.8 liters). Fed by a 2-barrel Stromberg downdraft carburetor, the 12-cylinder powerplant developed 150 hp (152 PS) at 3,800 rpm and 292 lb-ft (396 Nm) of torque at 1,200 rpm. Power reached the rear axle through a synchronized 3-speed manual transmission , enabling an effortless 90 mph (145 kph) top speed.
Carrying a base price of $4,700 for a standard Brunn Tourer Cabriolet and rising to $7,000 for semi-custom coachwork, the 1938 Lincoln Model K V12 competed against America's finest multi-cylinder flagships. While the supercharged 420-cubic-inch (6.9-liter) Duesenberg Model J delivered 265 hp (269 PS) to 320 hp (324 PS) and 115 mph (185 kph) performance for more than $15,000 across 481 chassis, Cord Corporation had already dissolved in 1937.
Photo: YouTube/Jay Leno's Garage Among surviving 1938 rivals, the Lincoln Model K occupied an exclusive middle ground in price, rarity, and output. The 1938 Packard Twelve, priced from $4,155 to $8,510, utilized a 473-cubic-inch (7.8-liter) V12 producing 175 hp (177 PS) and 366 lb-ft (496 Nm), outselling Lincoln with 566 units. Meanwhile, Cadillac built 315 examples of its Series 90, priced from $5,135 to $7,170 with a 431-cubic-inch (7.1-liter) 185-hp (188-PS) V16.
Only the moribund Pierce-Arrow Twelve proved rarer in 1938, assembling fewer than 30 total motorcars before bankruptcy, with its 462-cubic-inch (7.6-liter) V12 rated at 185 hp (188 PS) and 350 lb-ft (475 Nm) and priced from $3,895 to $5,015. Although outmuscled on paper by Cadillac, Packard, and Pierce-Arrow, the 414-cubic-inch Lincoln V12 excelled in mechanical silence, making Judkins's sole 1938 Touring Coupe an enduring monument to prewar American coachbuilding artistry.
The durability of that powerplant is beyond debate – even in 2026, when the episode for Jay Leno’s Garage YouTube series was filmed, the mighty Lincoln had no problem swooshing down the road at 60 mph. It won’t make a comfortable daily driver, but it will cruise on the open road like it owns it (and, looking at it gliding along, we can’t say it doesn’t).

2026 SEMA Show • Toyota Brings Fresh Adventure-Ready Concepts at the 2026 SEMA Show Under the Woodland Banner
This Corolla Cross EV Test Mule Features Toyota's New Multi-Pathway Vehicle Platform
15 photos
Photo: Baldauf
Toyota wants future electric vehicles, plug-in hybrids, and regular hybrids to share a common vehicle architecture. Said multi-pathway vehicle platform has to be flexible and modular enough to not force one powertrain to compromise another, and that's a seriously tall order when the full-electric version needs a substantial battery while hybrid vehicles have to accommodate oily bits.
This Corolla Cross-shaped prototype offers the first glimpse into the Japanese automaker's most ambitious vehicle platform yet. From the outset, it's exceedingly clear that we are looking at a test mule from the shortened wheelbase and the unusually high suspension. The way the high-voltage battery sticks out underneath also suggests test mule rather than production-intent prototype.
Back in October 2026, the world's largest automaker confirmed that it's developing a multi-pathway vehicle platform that can integrate hybrid powertrains without affecting interior space or capability. Toyota made a case for a lower-profile engine and hybrid package, enabling more dynamic proportions.
A new 1.5-liter engine with four pots arranged in a line is on the menu as well. Toyota has already confirmed naturally aspirated and turbo flavors, along with a target of 15 percent improved fuel economy in hybrid form. The 15 percent gain is expected to come from lower aerodynamic drag, hence the lower-profile engine and hybrid package, reduced electrical losses, improved thermal management, and lower mechanical friction.
Regarding the hybrid system, Toyota claims that it's smaller and more compact in every sense, down to the electric drive units, inverters, and power control units. As for the multi-pathway approach, the company wants to spread both production and development investment across higher combined volumes. Given the aforementioned, it's easy to understand why a small crossover makes so much sense in places like Europe and the Japanese market.
Photo: Baldauf From the looks of it, said test mule lands somewhere between the Yaris Cross and the Corolla Cross. The round headlights are hilarious in and of themselves, as they don't fit the outgoing model's styling at all. On closer inspection, the structure underneath the donor body panels gives away extensive modifications.
The absence of exhaust outlets also eliminates the possibility of a plug-in hybrid, and this EV-centric approach is very telling. After all, Toyota made a mess of its e-TNGA model family from the outset. Even today, after extensive updates, the bZ and related electric models leave much to be desired when compared to direct competition. To understand how far behind Toyota is, bear in mind that all e-TNGA models feature 400-volt electrical systems.
We do know Toyota has 800-volt systems under development, and 800 volts could very well be the norm for this new platform. Elsewhere, the hybrids and plug-in hybrids are being developed with renewable and carbon-neutral fuels in mind. Looking at the bigger picture, giving prospective customers a three-way choice is much better in every respect compared to forcing electrics onto everyone in order to align with unrealistic government policies.
Customer preferences matter a lot, and energy circumstances differ wildly between markets. While certain regions such as northern European countries favor electric vehicles, others continue to favor anything that runs on dinosaur juice. Even Chinese passenger vehicle customers are crazy about EREVs, which use an internal combustion engine as a generator for the high-voltage battery and electric drive units.
As it stands, this Corolla Cross test mule is telling us more about Toyota's immediate engineering priorities rather than the all-new crossover's exterior appearance. One could even argue that said model could replace both the Yaris Cross and the Corolla Cross, but alas, it's way too early to say for sure.
